0.bp: When you take a photo with your phone in bright sunlight next to a dark shadow, your camera has to choose: keep the sky white or show details in the shadow, but rarely both. Your eye handles this effortlessly because it sees about 20 stops of brightness levels (a "stop" is a doubling of brightness). This paper tackles the core problem of bringing that eye-like vision to smartphone cameras.
0.wh: Phone sensors today max out at about 12 stops of brightness range. Researchers have tried combining multiple exposures (taking the same scene at different brightnesses and merging them), which can squeeze out 3-5 extra stops. But the real trap is that current AI methods often hallucinate—they invent details that weren't actually captured, creating artifacts. You can't trust deep learning here without ground truth.
0.ap: Instead of trusting a neural network to imagine missing details, this method takes a more honest approach: every pixel in the final image is a weighted blend (a convex combination) of nearby pixels from the different exposures, adjusted for how dark or bright each exposure was. It's like mixing paints—if you combine 30% from a dark exposure and 70% from a bright one, you get something in between, not invented.
0.ww: This works because light is linear. If you have the raw pixel data from multiple cameras all pointing at the same scene, just at different exposure levels, you can safely mix them without cheating. The method avoids the brittleness of hallucination-based approaches and the method runs fast enough on your phone because it only does arithmetic, not big neural network inference.
0.po: The paper shows the method generalizes to real phones it never saw before, handling anywhere from 3 to 9 stacked photos. It also works well enough that it even improves other existing methods when you retrain them the same way, suggesting the training approach is robust. Your smartphone can now hold onto details in both blown-out skies and dark shadows without inventing things.

1.bp: When you have two 3D shapes and want to know how different they are, you compute the Hausdorff distance—the maximum gap between any point on one shape and the nearest point on the other. This matters for design verification, quality control in manufacturing, and collision detection. The trouble is computing it precisely and quickly, especially on modern graphics processors (GPUs).
1.wh: The standard computer-science approach (Branch-and-Bound) is sequential and relies on a priority queue—a data structure that sorts candidates to check next. This is fast on a single CPU core, but GPUs are massively parallel; they work best when thousands of tasks run simultaneously without waiting for each other. A global priority queue becomes a traffic jam—one core manages it while others sit idle.
1.ap: This paper throws away the priority queue and instead uses a ring buffer (a simple, lock-free circular array) to send work to thousands of GPU cores. The trick is relaxing the "best-first" ordering: instead of always checking the most promising candidates first, they process work in batches asynchronously. They also add a seven-stage filtering pipeline to quickly prune obviously empty regions so cores never even look there.
1.ww: Ordering doesn't actually matter for correctness if you filter enough. If you can eliminate whole regions as provably not-the-answer, you don't need to know which specific candidate is best next. By switching from sequential, ordered search to parallel, batch-ordered search, they turn a serial bottleneck into a high-throughput pipeline that feeds all GPU cores steadily.
1.po: The speedups are enormous: 71.7 times faster than the best CPU method on typical shapes, and over 10,000 times faster on tricky industrial CAD models. They also shrink the data for each task from many bytes to 29 bytes, saving memory bandwidth. This enables real-time shape comparison on the GPU, useful for interactive design and collision systems.

2.bp: Sand and water don't mix simply. When you pour water on dry sand, it flows through. When sand is fully soaked, it behaves like wet clay, sticky and heavy. Real beaches, riverbeds, and landslides involve complex feedback between flowing water, trapped air, and grains sliding and settling. Simulating this realistically is hard but matters for visual effects, environmental design, and understanding erosion.
2.wh: Most simulators treat water and sand separately. But they're deeply coupled: water changes how sand sticks together and moves, while sand changes how water flows. Separately simulating each and bolting them together creates artifacts—instability, incorrect settling, unrealistic erosion. A unified framework that handles both together needs a method that respects both the fluid flow equations and the granular mechanics.
2.ap: The paper uses two complementary numerical techniques: Lattice Boltzmann Method (LBM) for fluids—a way to simulate flowing, two-phase mixtures (water and air together) by tracking particle collisions on a grid, and Material Point Method (MPM) for granular material—which represents sand as particles moving through space and deforming as they go. A water retention model then describes how liquid clings to and fills the pores inside the granular structure.
2.ww: Combining them in a unified continuum (continuous) framework means both the fluid equations and the sand equations are written in the same language, so they naturally feed into each other. The water retention model is the key physical insight: it captures the transition from dry friction to wet stickiness by tracking how much water is absorbed. Volume conservation (tracking that matter doesn't vanish) stabilizes the whole system numerically.
2.po: The method handles complex real phenomena: sand washing away in floods, sediment settling to the bottom, erosion that undercuts banks. The paper validates on challenging scenarios like breaching a sand basin or a sand column collapsing into water. This opens the door to realistic effects for films and simulations of coastal or riverine disasters.

3.bp: Professional 3D modelers create shapes by hand, laying out faces (flat surfaces) in organized flows, keeping similar sizes, and aligning edges into neat strips called "quads" (four-sided faces) when possible. This organization matters not just for looks but for animation, UV mapping (how textures wrap), and subsequent tools downstream. Generating meshes that meet artist standards has been elusive because most AI methods produce chaotic, random-looking topology.
3.wh: Recent AI methods (transformers) generate 3D shapes by predicting faces one at a time in some sequence. The problem is choosing what order. If you sort by coordinates, sequences get long and rambling. If you use patches (groups of faces), you break the continuous flow of edges that professionals carefully craft. You get shapes that are geometrically okay but organizationally ugly—random-looking and hard to edit.
3.ap: This paper treats faces as tokens in a sequence inspired by triangle strips, a graphics technique where you chain faces along edges to minimize data. They construct the sequence as a connected walk through faces that explicitly marks UV boundaries (seams where textures wrap). The same sequence can be decoded as either triangles or quads, letting them train jointly on both data types.
3.ww: By honoring the edge flow naturally, they preserve the semantic layout (what parts belong together) that artists encode. The UV boundaries are explicit in the token sequence, so the model learns that edges flow coherently. Training on both triangles (lots of data) and quads (high quality) lets the model learn coarse structure from abundant data and refine into organized topology from curated examples.
3.po: Output meshes have better geometric quality, more coherent structure, and cleaner UV segmentation. This means artists spend less time hand-editing generated shapes and can integrate them faster into pipelines. The model respects professional conventions instead of violating them, making AI-assisted modeling actually usable in studios.

4.bp: Generative models (like diffusion, which gradually adds noise then removes it) can create sharp, realistic images, but they usually need many steps of denoising—sometimes 50 or more. If you want fast generation (one or two steps), you sacrifice quality. This paper asks: can we redesign the math so that few steps still work well?
4.wh: Traditional diffusion models think in terms of a corruption schedule: add noise for T steps, then remove it for T steps. Moving between timesteps is slow and must be done sequentially. If you skip steps to go faster, you lose quality because you're making big jumps in an ill-conditioned space. Rethinking this as a probability flow (how the data shifts through space) doesn't obviously help if you still take small, local steps.
4.ap: Instead of thinking about local, instant changes, they introduce cumulative flow maps—a concept from physics where you track how points move over finite time, not just infinitesimal time. A cumulative flow parametrization groups many steps into a single coherent motion. They apply this to both diffusion and flow-based generative models, changing how the model predicts and how time embeddings work.
4.ww: Cumulative flows let the model reason about large, global state changes instead of micro-steps. It's like moving from considering the next grain of sand to move toward mapping out the whole avalanche. The model can learn to make a big, coherent jump that maintains quality, rather than many tiny hops. The framework needs minimal architecture changes and no extra parameters.
4.po: Images, 3D shapes, and other data can now be generated in one or few steps with quality comparable to 50-step methods. This cuts inference time dramatically while keeping synthesis quality, enabling fast text-to-image or text-to-shape on devices and in interactive applications. The method is general—it works for images, shapes defined as implicit fields (SDFs), and even joint prediction tasks.

5.bp: The plenoptic function is the map of all light rays bouncing around a scene—for each direction looking from each spot, how bright is it? Capturing it fully reveals all the visual information about a scene. Time-resolved imaging (recording when light arrives) adds a temporal dimension, useful for seeing through fog or reconstructing 3D from light travel time. But sampling this huge space is practically impossible.
5.wh: The plenoptic function has five dimensions: two for camera position, two for viewing angle, and one for time. Sampling densely requires millions of measurements. Current systems couple illumination and viewing—you turn on a light and a camera sees it, but you can't independently control where light comes from and where you observe reflections. Many indirect light paths are blocked by occlusion (a nearby object hiding a far one).
5.ap: This paper decouples the laser (that sends light) from the detector (that measures it) so they can probe from different angles independently. They use a generative model—specifically, a 3D foundation model for initialization—to fill in the massive gaps from sparse samples. A differentiable transient path tracer (a physics simulator you can backpropagate through) refines the solution to match the few measurements you actually took.
5.ww: Foundation models come with strong 3D geometric priors (they've seen thousands of shapes and scenes), so they make reasonable guesses for unseen regions. The differentiable path tracer then tunes those guesses to be physically consistent with what you measured. Decoupling illumination and detection means you can shine light where a wall would block direct viewing, recovering indirect paths. The combination of learned priors and physics is more powerful than either alone.
5.po: The system captures high-dimensional light transport from sparse, practical measurements, recovering both visible and hidden regions. This enables new computational imaging: seeing through fog, capturing indirect reflections, reconstructing 3D transient phenomena. The generative framework elegantly bridges the gap between the measurements you can realistically take and the full information you want.

6.bp: Thin shells—cloth, paper, metal sheets, membranes—are everywhere in animation and design. They bend and fold convincingly when you simulate them correctly, but getting the mathematics right is surprisingly subtle. Different ways of breaking the continuous shell mathematics into discrete pieces (on a computer) give different results. Which one should you use?
6.wh: For decades, graphics researchers have proposed ten or more different discrete models for shell bending, with no consensus. Each makes different trade-offs: some are fast but inaccurate, some squeeze out precision but choke on sharp folds, some work on regular grids but fail on irregular meshes. Without careful comparison, it's unclear which to pick. And the literature doesn't give clear guidance on when a model breaks down.
6.ap: The paper tests all ten major models on three levels of challenge: an analytic benchmark (a shape with a known perfect answer) to measure convergence, a sharp-bend benchmark to see behavior at creases, and large-scale practical problems (hanging cloth, folding paper, dynamic draping). They measure accuracy, convergence as the mesh gets finer, and computational cost. They also identify gaps and propose new variants to fix them.
6.ww: Systematic testing reveals that different models shine in different contexts. Some converge smoothly as you refine the mesh; others have weird artifacts. Some handle dynamics well but fail at equilibrium. By comparing side-by-side, you see that the best model depends on your priorities (speed vs. accuracy) and your mesh type. New variants address specific failure modes.
6.po: Practitioners now have concrete guidance: which model to use for cloth vs. paper, when mesh quality matters, how much refinement you need. The paper identifies leading models and their tradeoffs, proposes new energy formulations, and gives practical algorithms. This removes guesswork from shell simulation, saving artists and engineers time and preventing unexpected failures.

7.bp: Simulating objects that collide—cloth tangling, sand piling, characters grabbing props—requires solving one big physics equation per frame: minimize energy (the cost of deformation, interpenetration, friction) subject to contacts not overlapping. This is robust and handles messy scenarios well. But it's also complex: adding new materials or collision types means re-deriving calculus by hand and rewriting code for each case.
7.wh: Current simulators hard-code specific energy types, shape types (spheres, capsules, meshes), and shape representations (parameterizations). If you want to add a new energy or mix different parameterizations in the same equation, you manually derive all first and second derivatives (a day of calculus) and hand-code the assembly logic. With many parameterization pairs, this explodes combinatorially.
7.ap: This paper introduces a symbolic framework (YASPS) that makes the structure of physics explicit in a computation graph. Two operators—JOIN (connectivity) and UNION (heterogeneous types)—encode which objects interact and how they're represented. Symbolic differentiation automatically computes all the derivatives you need. The sparsity pattern of the resulting matrix (which entries are nonzero) emerges automatically from the graph structure.
7.ww: You write the physics once in an abstract language, and the system automatically derives gradients and assembles the linear system. This is safe (derivatives are computed correctly) and maintainable (adding a new energy type means writing it once, not deriving and coding). The symbolic structure also reveals sparsity, so you never allocate memory for zero entries—a huge win for large systems.
7.po: Adding new energies, parameterizations, or material behaviors is now a matter of describing them symbolically, not hand-coding derivatives. This opens the door to rapid prototyping of new simulation physics and to systems that mix diverse parameterization (rigid bodies, deformable solids, cloth, each with its own representation) seamlessly. The framework removes a major barrier to experimentation.

8.bp: Modern graphics programs are orchestrations of thousands of parts: shaders (small programs on the GPU), buffers (blocks of data), pipelines (sequences of processing stages), and synchronization rules (when data is ready). These parts must agree on contracts: what type of data, what layout in memory, which GPU resources are bound where. Breaking a contract causes crashes or visual glitches that are hard to debug.
8.wh: Today, contracts are implicit—written in documentation or enforced by convention. A shader expects data in a buffer bound to location 5, but if the CPU code binds to location 4, there's no compile-time warning. The error emerges at runtime as corrupted visuals or cryptic validation failures. Catching these bugs requires careful testing and can be time-consuming for complex pipelines.
8.ap: RCGP formalizes contracts as explicit declarations, like type signatures in programming. Resources (buffers, textures, bindings) are declared in one central place. Program modules import and export these contracts. Combinators check that modules can connect—if one module outputs type A and the next expects type B, the composer catches it immediately. Witnesses enforce contracts at runtime.
8.ww: Making contracts explicit and centralizable means the compiler can check them statically (before running) instead of at runtime. If a contract breach happens, you get an error message pointing to the line, not a visual glitch after minutes of rendering. The central declaration avoids drift—you change the contract in one place, and the type checker ensures all modules see the same spec.
8.po: Graphics programmers catch resource contract bugs at development time, not in production. Visual artifacts from binding mismatches evaporate. The central declarations become documentation and reduce boilerplate. This is a quality-of-life improvement for teams writing large, modular graphics systems.

9.bp: Lattice metamaterials are lightweight structures made from tiny repeating unit cells—think of a honeycomb or a truss. They're strong, light, and can be tuned for vibration damping or thermal properties. Evaluating their effective properties (how stiff they are, how they respond overall) requires solving large equations on the unit cell. Doing this for each design candidate is slow, but you need speed to explore designs.
9.wh: Classical solver methods (like conjugate gradient or multigrid) are accurate but slow, especially for high-resolution metamaterials. Replacing them with neural networks is tempting for speed, but neural networks often lack physical rigor—they might give wrong answers or be unstable. You need both the speed of neural prediction and the certainty of numerical solvers.
9.ap: GMT combines a Transformer (a neural architecture that sees long-range relationships) with Geometric Multigrid, a classical solver technique that works on multiple resolutions simultaneously. The Transformer runs on the coarse and fine levels, predicting both the solution and correction terms (residuals) needed. Then one step of the classical multigrid algorithm refines the prediction to convergence.
9.ww: Multigrid accelerates solvers by smoothing at coarse scales and refining at fine scales. The Transformer mirrors this hierarchy, capturing dependencies across scales. Predicting both the solution and residual corrections gives the classical solver a good initialization, reducing iterations. Physics-aware positional encoding (encoding periodicity directly into the Transformer) ensures answers respect the material's periodic structure.
9.po: The hybrid method achieves residual errors under 1 part in 100,000 (high numerical accuracy) and runs 160 times faster than GPU-based classical solvers at equivalent accuracy. For high-resolution metamaterials (512×512×512), where classical methods are prohibitively slow, this enables interactive design exploration. The approach demonstrates that neural and classical numerics can be married for the best of both worlds.

10.bp: Rendering surfaces defined implicitly (as Gaussian process implicit surfaces—probabilistic descriptions of where surfaces are) allows rendering uncertainty and soft, fuzzy boundaries, useful for surfaces reconstructed from sensor noise. The catch is finding where rays hit the surface: you must march along the ray testing if you're inside the implicit surface, and each test is expensive because you must sample and evaluate Gaussian processes.
10.wh: Brute-force ray marching evaluates the implicit surface at every step along the ray, which is slow. If you can skip unnecessary steps or eliminate regions before reaching them, you save evaluations. Standard ray tracing uses bounding boxes to skip empty space, but implicit surfaces don't have a rigid boundary—they're probabilistic and fuzzy. It's unclear how to prune them safely.
10.ap: The paper derives mathematical bounds for Gaussian process implicit surfaces. Stratified Bernoulli impulses (a probabilistic technique) let you quickly bound whether a single ray point is likely to be near the surface, replacing expensive full evaluations. A region-level bound uses spatial acceleration structures to identify large patches of space that are probabilistically empty, so the ray marcher never checks them.
10.ww: Bounding works because Gaussian processes have structure: they're smooth and their variance changes predictably. You don't need to evaluate them densely; instead you prove that certain regions are too far from the surface and skip them. Two levels of bounds—point-level and region-level—cascade pruning: regions rules out large areas, point-level rules out remaining candidates.
10.po: Ray marching through implicit surfaces becomes much faster because evaluations are sparse. Overall rendering time improves substantially. This enables interactive rendering of probabilistic surfaces, useful for geometry from reconstruction algorithms that output uncertainty along with shape.

11.bp: Geometry processing algorithms (smoothing surfaces, parameterizing textures, deforming shapes) output 3D shapes or parameters. What if you want to use these outputs as objectives in machine learning? For instance, "minimize the distortion when texturing this mesh" as a loss function? You'd need to differentiate through the geometry algorithm—compute gradients of its output with respect to inputs. Current tools make this tedious.
11.wh: Geometry algorithms are complex: they involve iterative solvers (local-global methods, ADMM), matrix operations, and approximations tailored to geometry. Standard automatic differentiation frameworks (like PyTorch) can backpropagate through anything, but they're slow because they don't exploit structure. Geometry processing inherits efficiency through specialized solvers; automatic differentiation throws that away.
11.ap: Iskra differentiates through geometry algorithms by using the adjoint method (a classical technique for computing gradients through PDEs and solvers) on user-written imperative code. It exploits the structure of common solvers—the algorithm's sweep patterns, the block structure of matrices—to build an efficient backward pass. It integrates with machine learning frameworks but doesn't force you to rewrite the algorithm.
11.ww: The adjoint method is mathematically sound and efficient because it directly computes gradients without unnecessary computation. Tailor-made for iterative solvers, it avoids storing full computational history. Scatter-gather operations (the core of mesh processing) map cleanly to tensor operations, bridging the gap between imperative mesh algorithms and differentiable compute graphs.
11.po: You can now differentiate through existing geometry solvers (mean curvature flow, conformal parameterization, deformation, geodesic computation) without rewriting them. This opens applications in inverse geometry: given a desired property, optimize the input shape to achieve it. The low memory and fast runtimes let practitioners use geometry algorithms inside machine learning workflows.

12.bp: When filmmakers or game artists build a scene, they often start with a photograph of real terrain as reference: "I want mountains that look like this photo." Manually building a matching 3D terrain is slow and tedious. This paper asks: given a single photo, can you automatically generate a 3D heightmap (a 2D grid where each cell's height is the elevation) that matches the photo's view?
12.wh: From a single photo, you can only see what the camera points at. Terrain behind hills or outside the frame is invisible. Naively extracting 3D shape from the visible parts gives an incomplete terrain. A diffusion-based generative model can invent the hidden parts, but there's no guarantee the made-up terrain is plausible or consistent with the visible region.
12.ap: The method runs in two phases. First, it extracts the camera position and 3D point cloud from the image, converting that to a heightmap for visible areas. Second, it uses a diffusion model (trained on real elevation data) to fill in occluded regions. Three consistency checks guide the generation: geomorphological (hidden terrain resembles visible), hydrological (rivers flow realistically), and visual (rendering the result matches the input photo).
12.ww: The visible-part extraction is grounded in photo geometry—it doesn't hallucinate, just reconstructs captured data. For occluded regions, the diffusion model has seen real terrain and learned what elevation patterns are plausible. The three consistency principles anchor the solution: they prevent the invisible parts from being arbitrary or violating terrain physics. Rendering checks ensure the final terrain actually looks like the photo.
12.po: Artists can feed a reference photo and get a complete, renderable 3D terrain in minutes instead of hours. The heightmap integrates with standard scene authoring tools. The method handles various scales and terrain types. This bridges the gap between concept-art reference and functional 3D assets for games and films.

13.bp: Simulating multibody systems with mixed materials—rigid metal parts touching soft cloth and foam—is tricky on GPUs because each type needs different math. Stiff contacts (rigid bodies pressing together) and soft deformations (foam squashing) have very different time scales and behavior. A solver that works well for one often fails on the other.
13.wh: Standard Newton-Krylov solvers (iterative methods for large systems) converge slowly when the equation is ill-conditioned—when small changes in input cause huge changes in output. Mixed stiffness (some parts very stiff, others soft) creates terrible conditioning. GPU solvers must be matrix-free (avoiding storing huge matrices), but Krylov methods need good conditioning to converge fast.
13.ap: Heterogeneous Subspace Corrections splits the problem into two parts: a Newton-CG iteration for deformable bodies and a Neumann-based iteration for rigid-body contacts. A GPU-based Adaptive Cross Approximation algorithm exploits the low-rank structure of coupling matrices (the parts that connect deformable and rigid regions) to avoid expensive sparse matrix operations. A specialized data structure assembles contact forces in parallel.
13.ww: Splitting by material type decouples the ill-conditioning: each part has better conditioning on its own. Low-rank approximation of coupling means you don't multiply huge matrices; you work with compact representations. Parallel contact Hessian assembly (building the matrix describing contact forces) avoids serialization. Together, these transform a slow, ill-conditioned problem into a fast, well-structured computation.
13.po: Complex heterogeneous multibody systems now converge as quickly as direct solvers but run on GPUs and scale to high-resolution models with extensive contact. This enables real-time simulation of mixed-material scenes: rigid machinery interacting with cloth or foam, scenarios where prior GPU solvers would thrash or fail.

14.bp: 3D shapes have topology—holes, handles, cavities—independent of their exact geometry. Sometimes you want to simplify topology (remove holes) while keeping geometry (the shape's look) as unchanged as possible. This is useful for repairing noisy scans, preparing assets for animation, or ensuring shapes have certain structural properties. Existing methods either remove everything or give you little control.
14.wh: Topology is global structure: a shape's number of handles (donut holes), components (separate pieces), and voids (enclosed cavities). Simplifying it naively creates big geometric changes. And specifying exactly which topological features to keep is hard—you'd need to manually identify every hole you want. Automating this requires understanding which features matter and which can be discarded cheaply.
14.ap: The method uses persistent homology (a mathematical tool tracking which topological features are significant) to identify low-importance holes, handles, and voids. For each one marked for removal, it computes candidate cutting and filling operations (operations that would eliminate it). An efficient algorithm picks an optimal subset of candidates to minimize geometric change while hitting the target topology. An iterative refinement alternates between candidate suggestion and selection.
14.ww: Persistence measures whether a feature is "fleeting" (appears and disappears as you scan across the shape) or "robust" (lasts across many scales). Fleeting features are noise; robust ones are real. By removing only low-persistence features, the method discards noise-like artifacts and preserves intended structure. Candidate precomputation and optimal subset selection avoid exponential search.
14.po: Users specify the target number of components, handles, and voids, and the method simplifies the topology to match, making minimal geometric changes. This works on complex real shapes with hundreds of holes. The method is highly successful, making it practical for asset repair, scan cleanup, and ensuring structural properties needed downstream.
